content.title: Antiplatelet strategies to reduce bleeding risk in the first 12 months after ACS
content.figure: Figure 11: Alternative antiplatelet strategies to reduce bleeding risk in the first 12 months after an ACS. Diagram shows abbreviated DAPT strategies (1, 3, 6 month DAPT in HBR or non-HBR patients) and DAPT de-escalation strategies (potent P2Y12 inhibitor-based DAPT with aspirin + prasugrel or ticagrelor, with option to de-escalate to clopidogrel resulting in aspirin + clopidogrel; later P2Y12 inhibitor or aspirin monotherapy).
content.summary: Antiplatelet strategies to reduce bleeding risk in the first 12 months after ACS can be divided into abbreviated DAPT strategies and DAPT de-escalation strategies. Twelve-month DAPT (preferably with prasugrel or ticagrelor) remains the default for patients with ACS; abbreviated duration or de-escalation may be chosen to reduce bleeding risk (e.g., in HBR patients or when there are concerns regarding 12-month potent P2Y12 inhibitor-based DAPT). Choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and duration of DAPT should be individualized based on bleeding risk.
recommendations: Default strategy: 12-month DAPT with a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (prasugrel or ticagrelor) plus aspirin unless contraindicated.
Consider abbreviated DAPT (1, 3, or 6 months) in patients at high bleeding risk (HBR).
De-escalation option: switch from a potent P2Y12 inhibitor to clopidogrel (aspirin + clopidogrel) to reduce bleeding risk.
After abbreviated DAPT or de-escalation, continue either a P2Y12 inhibitor or aspirin as monotherapy up to 12 months as appropriate.

abbreviations.P2Y12: platelet P2Y12 receptor (target of P2Y12 inhibitors)

Associated Conditions: bleeding risk during antiplatelet therapy / DAPT
genes.context: Referred to throughout as 'P2Y12 inhibitor' or 'potent P2Y12 inhibitor-based DAPT'; de-escalation strategies involve changing from a potent P2Y12 inhibitor to clopidogrel, and choice/duration of P2Y12 inhibitor is highlighted as important for bleeding-risk management in ACS.
